questions.q: A project's package.json has "type": "module". Which files are CommonJS?
questions.explain: .cjs is always CommonJS and .mjs always ESM. .js follows the nearest package.json "type", here "module".
options: Files that use require, whatever their extension
None; CommonJS is not allowed in such a project

questions.q: A package.json has no "type" field. How does Node.js 24 treat a .js file in that package?
questions.explain: No "type" means CommonJS by default, with syntax detection as a fallback. Setting "type" explicitly avoids the guess and the warning.
options: As CommonJS, unless the file uses ESM syntax that cannot be CommonJS, in which case Node guesses ESM and warns

questions.q: Why can an ES module import not be placed inside an if block?
questions.explain: The parse and link phases need to know every import without running code. For a conditional load, use await import(…).
options: Because if blocks are not allowed in modules
Imports are found by parsing, before any code runs, so they must be static top-level declarations; import() is the dynamic form
It is allowed; only exports are restricted

questions.q: An ES module starts with console.log("start") and then imports a name that the other module does not export. What happens?
questions.explain: Linking connects every imported name before evaluation. A missing export stops the whole graph from running. CommonJS, by contrast, would run until the missing value was used.
options: "start" is printed, then a ReferenceError when the name is used
Nothing is printed: loading fails with a SyntaxError during linking, before any module code runs
The name is undefined and the program continues

questions.q: This CommonJS-style code destructures a function that the module does not export. What does it print?
questions.explain: With require, you get an ordinary object, and destructuring a missing property gives undefined without complaint. The mistake only surfaces when the value is called, which is what CommonJS code does in practice.

questions.q: What is this at the top level of a file?
questions.explain: ES modules run in strict mode without a module object. CommonJS wraps each file in a function called with this set to module.exports.
options: undefined in an ES module; module.exports in a CommonJS file

questions.q: An ES module needs the folder it lives in. __dirname is not defined there. What should it use?
questions.explain: process.cwd() is where the process was started, which is often a different folder. import.meta describes the current module.

questions.q: This file is an ES module. What does it print?
questions.explain: Modules are always strict, and in strict mode assigning to an undeclared name throws instead of creating a global. A CommonJS file without "use strict" would have created the global.

questions.q: An ES module imports from itself to show how imports behave. What does it print?
questions.explain: An import is a live binding to the exporter's variable, not a copy. Each record() updates the variable, and the imported name shows the current value. (Importing a module from itself is only a trick to fit the demonstration into one file.)

questions.q: This simulates what destructuring a require result does. What does it print?
questions.explain: The object got a copy of count when it was built, and destructuring copied it again. Only the module's own variable changed. That is why CommonJS state must be read through a function or a property that is updated, while ESM imports are live.

questions.q: Code does import { vatRate } from "./config.js"; and later vatRate = 0.1;. What happens?
questions.explain: Imports are views, not variables of the importer. If other modules must be able to change a value, the owner exports a function that does it.
options: The rate changes for every module
A TypeError: imported bindings are read-only; only config.js can change its own variable

questions.q: An ES module does import { refund } from "./payments.cjs" and gets "Named export 'refund' not found", although refund is on module.exports at run time. Why?
questions.explain: ESM needs export names at link time. The default import (import payments from "./payments.cjs") always works, and then you destructure the object.
options: CommonJS files cannot be imported from ESM
Node finds CommonJS named exports by scanning the source for simple patterns before the file runs; refund was added in a way the scan cannot see (for example in a loop)

questions.q: What does the default import of a CommonJS module give you?
questions.explain: Importing CommonJS from ESM always maps module.exports to the default import. That is why import pkg from "old-lib" is the reliable form.

questions.q: In Node.js 24, a CommonJS file calls require("./money.js"), where money.js is an ES module with export default and export const VAT_RATE. What does it get?
questions.explain: require(esm) is synchronous and returns the namespace object, as long as nothing in the module's graph uses top-level await.
options: An error: CommonJS cannot load ESM
The module's namespace object: VAT_RATE as a property and the default export under .default

questions.q: require("./settings.js") throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. What does that tell you, and what works instead?
questions.explain: require must return immediately, and a module that awaits at the top level cannot finish immediately. import() is asynchronous and always works.
options: The file does not exist; fix the path
settings.js (or something it imports) uses top-level await, so it cannot be loaded synchronously; use await import("./settings.js")
The file is CommonJS; rename it to .mjs

questions.q: Why is adding a top-level await to a published library a breaking change?
questions.explain: Top-level await belongs in application entry points and small config modules. Libraries should expose an explicit async setup function instead.
options: Top-level await is not allowed in libraries
CommonJS users who load the library with require start getting ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE, and every importer's startup now waits for it
It changes all exports to promises

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Top-level await is allowed in ES modules. The module pauses at the await, and anything that imports it would wait too.
options: SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions

questions.q: Which specifier is a bare specifier?
questions.explain: A bare specifier is a package name, optionally with a subpath. It is found through node_modules and the package's "exports" map. node: names are built-ins.

questions.q: In an ES module, import { toNaira } from "./money" fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND although money.js exists. Why?
questions.explain: CommonJS tries .js, .json and /index.js. ESM, like browsers, resolves exactly what you wrote.
options: ES modules cannot import from the same folder
ESM does not guess extensions or index.js; relative specifiers must name the file exactly: "./money.js"

questions.q: A file at /app/src/orders/create.js imports "zod". Where does Node.js look first?
questions.explain: Resolution walks up from the importing file's folder. That is how a monorepo root node_modules can serve many packages, and how nested folders can hold different versions.
options: /app/src/orders/node_modules/zod, then each parent folder's node_modules in turn
In a global folder of installed packages

questions.q: A package's "exports" lists only "." and "./money". What happens to import "shop-core/src/internal/rates.js" from another package?
questions.explain: The exports map is the package's public API. Internal files can be moved or renamed without breaking anyone, because nobody outside can import them.
options: It works, because the file exists
It fails with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED: only listed subpaths are reachable

questions.q: An exports entry is { "default": "./a.js", "import": "./b.js" }. What does import load?
questions.explain: Node takes the first matching condition. "default" matches everything, so it must come last.
options: ./a.js: conditions are checked in the order written, and "default" always matches

questions.q: What is the "imports" field (names starting with #) in package.json for?
questions.explain: # specifiers resolve through the package's own "imports" map and are not available to other packages.
options: Private aliases that code inside the package can use, such as #rates, so internal paths can change in one place

questions.q: An app imports shop-errors (ESM build) while an older dependency requires it (CJS build). An error thrown by the dependency fails err instanceof PaymentError in the app. Why?
questions.explain: This is the dual package hazard. Ship one implementation, or check errors by name, a code or a Symbol.for brand, which work across copies.
options: Two builds were loaded, so there are two different PaymentError classes
The error was not thrown correctly

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A module is evaluated once per specifier and cached. Importing it again, statically or with import(), returns the same namespace object with the same values.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: import() returns a promise for the namespace object. The default export is the default property.

questions.q: A route does await import(`./carriers/${req.query.carrier}.js`). What is wrong?
questions.explain: Importing runs a file's code with full permissions. Never build a specifier from input you do not control.
options: Template literals cannot be used with import()
The request chooses which file runs; ../ can reach outside the folder. Map names through an allow-list before importing
Nothing, as long as the file exists

questions.q: When should a service load its plugins with import()?
questions.explain: Loading at startup turns deployment mistakes into startup errors instead of slow or failing customer requests.
options: On each request, so new plugins are picked up immediately
Once during startup, failing fast if none load and logging the ones that failed
Never; plugins must be static imports

questions.q: Modules format.js and tax.js import each other. tax.js runs first and calls formatNaira, a function declaration exported by format.js. What happens?
questions.explain: Hoisted function declarations are ready as soon as the module is linked. A const arrow function or a class would still be in the temporal dead zone and throw.
options: It works: function declarations are initialised during linking, before any module body runs

questions.q: This simulates reading a const that another module in a cycle has not initialised yet. What does it print?
questions.explain: A const exists from the start of its scope but cannot be read until its line runs: the temporal dead zone. An ESM import in a cycle points at such a binding, which is why the error is "Cannot access … before initialization".

questions.q: A CommonJS app crashes with TypeError: Class extends value undefined is not a constructor or null right after someone added a require. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: In a cycle, require returns the half-finished exports object. Destructuring copies undefined, and extends undefined fails.
options: A syntax error in the class
A circular require: the base class was destructured from a module.exports that was still empty because its module had not finished loading
The class name is misspelled in the error

questions.q: Which change does not remove a circular dependency?
questions.explain: File names do not matter; the direction of imports does. The first three make the dependencies point one way or delay the lookup until both modules have loaded.
options: Moving what both modules need into a third module
Passing the dependency in as a function argument
Looking the other module up inside the function that needs it, at call time

questions.q: This small simulation of CommonJS's cache shows what a cycle hands out. What does it print?
questions.explain: base is put in the cache before it runs. When card requires it back, it gets base's still-empty exports, so Base is undefined there, even though it exists once base finishes.

questions.q: Why does import { z } from "zod" fail when a browser loads the file directly with <script type="module">?
questions.explain: Node's resolution algorithm is a Node feature. In browsers, bundlers resolve bare specifiers at build time, or an import map maps them to URLs.
options: Browsers do not support ES modules
Browsers resolve specifiers as URLs and have no node_modules lookup; a bare name needs an import map or a bundler
Named imports are not allowed in browsers

questions.q: Write resolveSubpath(exportsMap, subpath, condition) that mimics a simplified "exports" lookup: find the entry for subpath; if it is a string, return it; if it is an object of conditions, return the first entry (in order) whose key is condition or "default". If nothing matches, throw an Error with the message ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED SUBPATH.
questions.explain: Conditions are tried in the order written, so a "default" placed first wins even for import. Anything not in the map is refused, which is how packages hide their internals.

questions.q: Write carrierPath(name) for a plugin loader: return the module path for a known carrier from the KNOWN map, and throw an Error with the message not an allowed carrier: NAME for anything else, including inherited keys like toString.
questions.explain: An allow-list maps trusted names to paths, so configuration or request data never becomes part of a path. Object.hasOwn ignores inherited keys such as toString.
questions.expected:
./carriers/gig.js
not an allowed carrier: ../../etc/passwd
not an allowed carrier: toString
./carriers/kwik.js

questions.q: A module graph maps each file to the files it imports. Write findCycle(graph, start) that returns the first import cycle reachable from start as an array of names ending with the repeated one (for example [ 'a', 'b', 'a' ]), or null if there is none. Use depth-first search with the current path.
questions.explain: A node that appears again on the current path closes a cycle; a node already fully explored cannot lead to a new one. This is what tools such as madge do over your real imports.

questions.q: Write lazy(load): it returns a function that calls load() (which returns a promise, like import()) the first time it is called, and returns the same promise on every later call, so the module is only loaded once even when two callers ask at the same time.
questions.explain: Storing the promise, not the result, is what makes simultaneous callers share one load. import() itself caches modules, but a wrapper like this is useful when loading also involves setup work.

questions.q: Simulate an ES module importing a CommonJS module: write importCjs(moduleExports, detectedNames) that returns a namespace object with default set to moduleExports, plus one property for each name in detectedNames (the names Node's scan found). Show that refund, added dynamically, is only reachable through default.
questions.explain: Named exports from CommonJS are only those the static scan detected; the default export is always the whole module.exports. That is why import pkg from "./x.cjs" is the dependable form.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ES modules only load JSON when you say so with the import attribute type: "json" (statically: import settings from "./settings.json" with { type: "json" }). The data becomes the default export.

questions.q: This file is an ES module run by Node.js. What does it print?
questions.explain: require, module and __dirname are provided to CommonJS files only. ES modules use import, import(), import.meta and, when needed, createRequire(import.meta.url).
questions.code: console.log(typeof require, typeof module, typeof __dirname, typeof import.meta.url);

questions.q: Node detects CommonJS named exports by scanning source text. Write a tiny version: detectExports(source) returns the names assigned with the literal patterns exports.NAME = or module.exports.NAME =, in order, without duplicates. Names added any other way are not detected.
questions.explain: capture is assigned through a computed key in a loop, so no text pattern can know its name without running the code. That is exactly the case where an ES module must use the default import of a CommonJS file.
